articles.title: Is “Dolly Parton Day” Coming Our Way on 9/25? Here’s What’s Happening This Year and (Hopefully!) Beyond
articles.content:
近日，传奇歌手多莉·帕顿（Dolly Parton）以80岁高龄去世，人们虽对各种议题意见分歧，但对她的赞誉却异常一致。她一生以音乐、欢乐和善举回馈世界，尽管这个世界并不总是回报她。

全球各地的致敬声不绝于耳：英国国王查尔斯三世安排皇家卫队在白金汉宫外演奏《9到5》，田纳西大学足球队将在2026年球季期间在头盔上印上多莉的名字，纳什维尔机场甚至有改名的计划。此外，9月25日可能成为“多莉·帕顿日”，纪念她逝世一周年。这一日期的选择别具匠心，因为“9-2-5”正是她经典歌曲《9到5》的发布日期（1980年11月3日），这首歌以其对劳动者的讴歌成为时代经典，曾获两项格莱美奖（最佳乡村歌曲及最佳女演唱者），并入围奥斯卡最佳原创歌曲奖，最终失之交臂，输给《名声》中的《Fame》。

目前，多莉·帕顿日的定位更类似社交媒体或民间纪念日，但加州已正式将9月25日定为“多莉·帕顿日”，其他城市也纷纷以各自方式纪念她。虽联邦层面的假期可能遥遥无期，但粉丝们仍期待这个日子能得到更广泛认可。

著名乡村歌手盖思·布鲁克斯（Garth Brooks）和媳妇特里西亚·耶伍德（Tricia Yearwood）也行动起来，宣布将他们的纳什维尔酒吧“低调的朋友”（Friends in Low Places Bar & Honky Tonk）当天的全部收入捐给儿童识字事业。多莉的“想象图书馆”（Imagination Library）计划向全球儿童赠送数百万册书籍，纪念她从未学会读书的父亲。

多莉·帕顿的遗产团队宣布，原定为她80岁生日的庆典“多莉节”（Dollyfest）将于2027年在纳什维尔和伦敦同时举办，以庆祝她的生命，而非传统追悼会。多莉的家人强调，最好的纪念方式是延续她的识字事业，她在个人网站上说：“我们已走过很长的路，但还有更多要做，让我们共同实现这个梦想，让所有儿童都能在书香满屋中成长。”

此外，多莉的家乡田纳西州塞维尔县也将推出“追随多莉的脚步”专题游览路线，带领游客重温她的成长经历。多莉·帕顿主题公园“多莉之家”（Dollywood）虽未专门为9月25日举办活动，但将举办秋季收获节和5公里赛跑，并计划在园内增设雕塑、瀑布等纪念设施。
articles.summary:
People never agree on anything these days, but they sure seem to agree on Dolly Parton, who died last week at the age of 80. And why wouldn’t they? She spent her life bringing music, joy and kindness to a world that doesn’t always give back in return.

Tributes are coming in from all over the world, from King Charles, who had the royal guard play “9 to 5” outside Buckingham Palace, to the University of Tennessee football team, who will celebrate Dolly on their helmets during the 2026 season. Plans are even underway to rename the Nashville airport in her honor.

And now, there’s news that we might be getting a Dolly Parton Day on Sept. 25. That day will mark the one-month anniversary of the icon’s death, and we can’t think of a more appropriate day to celebrate. If you’re scratching your head at the significance, keep reading as we explore why this might actually happen.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more celebrity news, cleaning, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.

How does a day become a designated holiday?

It depends on the holiday.

For something like Christmas or the 4th of July, it takes congressional action, and we have only 12 of these federal celebrations. (Juneteenth was the last one added to the calendar, in 2021.) There are also patriotic and national observances, like Flag Day and Arbor Day, which require Congressional approval as well. The country currently has 49 of these, which unfortunately do not come with a day off work.

Then there are the fun ones, like May the 4th (be with you), which honors Star Wars, and Dec. 23’s Festivus, a cheeky protest alternative to Christmas. These just kind of spread by word of mouth. Social media and the mainstream press get a lot of mileage out of these unofficial “holidays,” and they honor everything from pizza to pi (aka 3.14, which is also the date it’s observed).

For now, a day dedicated to Dolly mostly falls into the third category, though at least one state is jumping on the official train as we speak. California just officially declared Sept. 25 Dolly Parton Day, and cities and towns across the country are celebrating in their own ways (more on these coming up). A federal holiday might be too much to ask for with this Congress, but cross your fingers, Dolly fans!

Why would 9/25 be the perfect day for this?

It’s truly an inspired choice, and all you have to do is say the date as numbers to know why: 9-2-5. Get it? Dolly’s anthem to working people everywhere, “9 to 5” gets our toes tapping just as much now as it did when it was released on Nov. 3, 1980, ahead of the movie of the same name starring Dolly, Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin.

The song won two Grammys (Best Country Song and Best Country Vocal Performance, Female) and was nominated for an Academy Award for Best Song. It lost to another movie-title song, Irene Cara’s “Fame,” which is also pretty great. But let’s be real—how many people are watching that flick on repeat these days?

What is happening this year on 9/25 in honor of Dolly?

Garth Brooks and Tricia Yearwood are spearheading this one. They just announced that they will donate the entire day’s proceeds from their Nashville bar, Friends in Low Places Bar & Honky Tonk, to children’s literacy. As you probably know, Dolly’s Imagination Station sends millions of books to children around the world in honor of her father, who never had the chance to learn to read.

Here are other official Dolly Day declarations and tributes happening this Sept. 25, but rest assured, it’s not an exhaustive list. The idea to set aside a special day for Dolly seems to be gaining steam, so check back soon.

  • New Orleans: Mayor Helena Moreno declared 9/25 Dolly Day, and the city will host a parade in true NOLA fashion. The Krewe of Dolly, known for sporting Dolly wigs and fashion, will be the headliner. (Krewes are social clubs that build floats and otherwise participate in Mardi Gras.)
  • Lexington, Kentucky: The city will host a free event on 9/25, and donations will go to the Imagination Library. “Come dressed in your best Dolly-inspired sparkle and let’s celebrate her the way she lived—with love, laughter, music and a whole lot of heart,” the invite says.
  • Cocke County, Tennessee: In his last official act as mayor, Rob Mathis declared Sept. 25 Dolly Parton Day in the county. State lawmakers are considering similar actions.
  • Manhattan, New York: Borough president Brad Hoylman-Sigal declared Sept. 25 Dolly Parton Appreciation Day.

Bar crawls, library events and other less official celebrations are also planned, so check around in your hometown—or organize your own!

  • Chattanooga, Tennessee: Plant Bar Chattanooga will host a Dolly Day from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m, where fans can color Dolly-inspired pages and purchase butterflies for $1 to place at an altar in her honor. All proceeds benefit the Imagination Library.
  • Loveland, Colorado: Fans from all over northern Colorado will gather in downtown Loveland for the Dolly Parton Bar Crawl on 9/25. It starts at 9 a.m. and goes until 5 p.m., naturally.
  • Baton Rouge, Louisiana: The public library will host an event on 9/25 featuring a screening of 9 to 5 as well as a costume contest and a chance to enroll in or support Dolly’s Imagination Library.

Has Dollywood announced any plans yet?

Not specifically for 9/25, though the theme park will be hosting a Harvest Festival and a 5K race that were already in the works. In keeping with Dolly’s business-minded approach to life, Dollywood also remained open after her death, saying “the show must go on.”

Dollywood president Eugene Naughton recently announced plans to honor the theme park’s “dreamer-in-chief” with updates around the park, including a sculpted guitar and waterfall, as well as a planned 11-stop walking tour, “In Dolly’s Footsteps,” around Sevierville, Tennessee.

While not a Dollywood event, Dolly Parton’s estate announced that Dollyfest, a worldwide celebration that was originally planned as an 80th birthday party for the artist, will take place simultaneously in Nashville and London sometime in 2027. Organizers say that Dolly wanted this to be a celebration of life, not a traditional memorial, so mark your calendars for a party.

What are some ways you can celebrate Dolly’s life and legacy?

Dolly’s family says the most important thing you can do to honor Dolly is to continue her mission of literacy. “It’s been quite a journey, but we have so much more left to do,” she says on her website. “Let’s share this dream that all children should grow up in a home full of books.”

Here are ways you can help with that goal and others near to her heart:

  • Literacy and education: Donate to the Imagination Library, the Dollywood Foundation (which gives scholarships to older students) or your local libraries and schools. Just one of her scholarship efforts reduced dropout rates in Sevier County, Tennessee, from 35% to 6%.
  • Medical research: Dolly famously donated $1 million to vaccine research during the COVID-19 pandemic, and she also proudly received her vaccine in public (singing “vaccine, vaccine” to the tune of “Jolene”) to spread the word on the importance of getting vaccinated.
  • Disaster relief: When her home state and county suffered devastating wildfires in 2016, Dolly gave $1,000 per month to affected families, which ended up pumping $12.7 million into the county’s economy.
  • Wildlife protection: Dollywood houses a 30,000-square-foot aviary that rehabilitates and houses bald eagles that can’t be released into the wild.

Sources:

  • Congress.gov: “Congressional Recognition of Commemorative Days, Weeks, and Months: Background and Current Practice”
  • NOLA.com: “New Orleans parade krewe moves Dolly Parton celebration of life to later this month”
  • Garth Brooks: “Friends in Low Places Bar & Honky-Tonk Declares September 25 ‘Dolly Day’ to Support Imagination Library and Children’s Literacy”
  • New York Times: “Dolly Parton’s Other Legacy: A Fortune Given Away, Dollar by Dollar”
  • Fox 8 Live: “New Orleans to declare ‘Dolly Day’ with 9/25 celebration”
  • California Senate: “Senators Grove and Laird honor Dolly’s Literacy Legacy, Make 9/25 Dolly Parton Day in California”
  • Dolly Parton: “DOLLYFEST: The Celebration of A Lifetime Star-Studded Two-Day Festival Honoring Dolly Parton to Take Place in 2027”
  • Attractions Magazine: “Dollywood announces Dolly Parton tributes: New character, chapel area and exhibit”
  • Imagination Library: “Dollywood Foundation”

articles.title: This Monthly Book Subscription is Like BookTok—But Better
articles.content:
Ever wonder why reading gets harder as you get older? If you’re anything like us, finding your next great read, especially right after finishing a book you completely adored, is exhausting. Sure, you can always pick up a random new release and hope for the best. But let’s be honest—that strategy often ends with a $30 novel you’ll never crack open.
That’s where a book subscription box comes to the rescue!
Instead of agonizing over vague back-cover summaries and hunting down non-spoiler reviews, book club members hand over the reins to someone else to pick their next page-turner. This adds a delightful element of surprise to a TBR (to-be-read) pile, but it can also backfire hard if you get stuck with a dud.
That’s why we love Book of the Month (BOTM), which offers a fun, non-traditional twist on the classic book subscription box model. Not only do readers get to choose their own reads from a short list of buzzy new releases each month, but they also get some peace of mind knowing that the books are all pre-vetted by fellow readers. No more wasting time or money on a flop? Sign us up!
Book of the Month makes finding your next great read easy with a curated selection of buzzy new releases each month.
Book of the Month Club is similar to other monthly book clubs, but with a major plot twist. Rather than receiving a randomly chosen book each month, subscribers pick from a curated lineup of five or six new release titles. Each option comes from a popular or up-and-coming author and is pre-vetted by the BOTM team. That means only top-tier new releases make this exclusive cut—a big reason why it appeals to bookworms like Senior Editor Katie Bandurski.
“In 2024, I made it my personal mission to start actively reading again,” says Katie. “Like most 20-somethings, I started with the recommendations plaguing my Instagram feed. One or two picks were really good, a few were truly terrible and most landed somewhere in the middle. Sick of spending money on subpar reads, I started looking for a better source—and that’s when I found Book of the Month.”
BOTM works on a credit-based system. Each month, subscribers receive one monthly credit for $17.99 plus tax, which is redeemable for one book. There’s also an option to pay $14.99 per credit for a two-credit plan, or $13.99 per credit for 12 credits per year if you want to save a little cash.
Handy gift subscription are available for $59.99 (three books), $99.99 (six books), or $199.99 (12 books) make it a super easy and thoughtful gift for readers, too. You can also pick from audiobooks instead, if that’s more your speed!
Katie initially tested Book of the Month for three months in 2024—July, August, and September. Setting up an account is quick, easy, and completely painless. Just navigate to the signup page and enter all the standard details—shipping address, payment info, and a password.
Next, you choose your book from the aforementioned shortlist of titles. Each subsequent month, subscribers receive an email reminding them to choose a new book. From her very first book onward, Katie was hooked.
“I liked that Book of the Month doesn’t pigeonhole itself into specific genre recommendations every month,” says Katie. “In August, for example, there were no historical fiction titles. But in July, there were two. This makes me feel they are truly recommending the best of the best in new releases.”
As a member, you can also add selections from previous months to your box at a discount and cast a vote for the coveted “Book of the Year” award. And if you’re just not feeling the vibe of the current books, you can skip a month and redeem your credit later.
Given that each month’s list includes only new releases, the lineup always feels fresh. While one month might lean into a specific genre, the next month will have a completely new collection to explore. It really is a fun surprise every single time!
“I LOVE to read. But I’m not a huge library goer,” says Katie. “I love the idea of selected, vetted books from a source I can trust. And I also like still being able to choose which one I want rather than an AI algorithm selecting for me.”
Katie originally planned on testing the service for only three months. But after missing her curated picks, she retested it roughly a year later in May, June and July 2025 to ensure the service holds up.
While not every book was a fast favorite, most months were winners. One of her favorite finds was Husbands & Lovers by repeat author Beatriz Williams, a historical fiction spanning multiple generations of women.
“When my book arrived in a bright blue box, I was eager to dive in. And it’s a good thing I had a free weekend because this book was impossible to put down. I read it cover to cover in 24 hours. The character depth, story development and timeline jumps had me hooked from the first page.”
But our favorite aspect of a Book of the Month subscription? The price point, especially for hardback new releases, is very affordable. So even if you don’t absolutely love every pick, it’s still better than buying a random novel at full price. Plus, the books are specially designed to look cohesive when displayed together, which is a nice attention to detail.
“These titles aren’t the same trade hardback books you’d pick up at Barnes & Noble,” says Katie. “Each cover includes a Book of the Month logo on the dust jacket, as well as an embellishment with the month and year on the cover. The books are all a standard size, too, for easy display on your bookcase.”
Content Director Nicole Doster and Shopping Editor Mary Henn both gave BOTM subscriptions as gifts during the 2024 holiday season, and both received rave reviews from family and friends.
“I gifted a three-month subscription to my mother-in-law who always has her nose in a book,” says Nicole. “The gifting process was seamless, and I appreciated that they had an option for a physical gift card so I didn’t show up to Christmas empty-handed. I even got a notification when she signed up!”
Mary had a similar experience. “I needed a gift for the family member who ‘has everything’ and also loves books—and BOTM was the perfect find,” she explains. “With BOTM, she can choose books she doesn’t already own from a curated list. Buying a subscription as a gift is super easy too! I opted for a physical card, which tucked in a little gift basket with other goodies.”
Even I became a fan after trying it out for three months. In fact, Book of the Month introduced me to two of my current favorite writers. As someone who is usually hesitant to explore new-to-me authors, that’s a pretty big deal.
For folks like me who suffer from choice paralysis, having a curated collection of new, pre-vetted stories to choose from makes finding new favorites a total breeze. And who knows—you may find a new favorite author or two!
Skip the guesswork and discover your next page-turner from a selection of books pre-vetted by fellow readers.
At just $17.99 per book, Book of the Month subscribers enjoy these hardcovers for well below retail price at places like Barnes & Noble or even Amazon. Plus, Book of the Month often offers a first-time-subscriber promotion that scores you your first book for just $9.99! If BookTok has betrayed you one time too many, it’s time to turn to the experts.
What’s more, it makes a great low-effort, high-impact gift for bookworms, to boot!
If you prefer something closer to a traditional book club—complete with a dedicated Facebook group for lively discussions—try the Reader’s Digest Fiction Favorites club. Subscribers are treated to a special published volume filled with four condensed books from popular and upcoming authors seven times a year. Because the books arrive edited for length, they offer a faster reading experience, too.
As Senior Shopping Editor at Reader’s Digest, Katie Bandurski has been researching and reviewing gifts and subscription services for over five years. Her recommendations include coffee subscriptions, puzzle clubs, flower delivery and candle of the month boxes. In her personal time, she’s also an avid reader with a penchant for historical fiction, romance and fantasy titles.
The post This Monthly Book Subscription is Like BookTok—But Better appeared first on Reader's Digest.

articles.title: Happy Birthday, Keanu Reeves! 35 Unforgettable Quotes That Show Exactly Why We Love Him
articles.content:
Some celebrities have fans. Keanu Reeves has what feels like the entire internet rooting for him. Maybe it’s the action-hero cool, the endlessly quotable movies or the fact that, after decades of fame, he still comes across as someone you’d genuinely want to grab a coffee with. Whatever the reason, our collective love for Keanu runs deep—and with his birthday on Sept. 2, there’s no better time to revisit some of the best Keanu Reeves quotes.
Reeves got his start acting in the 1980s before winning over audiences in Bill & Ted’s Excellent Adventure and, eventually, becoming the blockbuster star behind movies like Speed, The Matrix and John Wick. To celebrate his big day, we’ve rounded up our favorite quotes from his most popular films and best interviews. Some will make you laugh, some will inspire you and a few will probably make you want to plan a Keanu movie marathon immediately. (We support this decision.)
Read on for the best Keanu Reeves quotes, and prepare to love him just a little bit more.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more quotes, entertainment, fun facts, humor, travel and tech all week long.
Best Keanu Reeves quotes
- “It’s easy to stay grounded. The ground is very close. And we walk on it every day.”
- “It’s fun to be hopelessly in love. It’s dangerous, but it’s fun.”
- “I think that a picture can tell a thousand words, and none of them can be right. Or true.”
- “Try and respect others. Try and continue to get the most out of life, and find ways to get that in this situation but also to respect it. Find ways to connect if you can. I mean, just … survive.”
- “I guess it’s just to my tastes to keep life as simple as I can.”
- “I don’t have kids or anything like that, so I get to be less responsible! The day is kind of like, ‘What, creatively, can I do?’”
- “Grief changes shape, but it never ends.”
- “Kissing someone is pretty intimate—actually, very intimate—and your heart always kind of skips a beat before you do that.”
- “Honestly, I try not to do anything I don’t want to do.”
- “All of these characters have some DNA of mine—I share it with the character.”
- “Once in a while, I have the moments where you drink the whiskey and you get the records out and you start doing the DJ thing until 4 in the morning.”
- “I’m always looking for catharsis.”

articles.title: These Are the Best—And Worst—Times for Avoiding Labor Day Weekend Traffic
articles.content:
Gas prices are high right now, but end-of-summer travel must go on. At least, that’s what your kids, friends and the hospitality industry hope to hear. It might be rougher than usual: Prices are up across the board for fuel, hotels and airfare, according to AAA (and your powers of simple observation).
But let’s focus on driving, because that’s why you’re here, right? Labor Day travel is a great way to ease into fall before the school year really gets going—if you can swing it. Last year, the average national price for a gallon of gas was $3.19, and this year, it’s $4.10 as of this writing. Hotel prices are up 9%, so short road trips might rule the day.
Are you headed out on the road this weekend? Even with higher prices, Chase Travel reports that domestic bookings are up 17%. If you’ve scrimped and saved for one last hurrah, the only thing left to worry about is the traffic. Well, AAA and INRIX teamed up to map out the best and worst times to drive this weekend, as well as which routes will be the most clogged. Fill up that tank, pack your trunk and read on to find out how to avoid Labor Day weekend traffic.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more travel, cleaning, humor, tech and fun facts all week long.
Every year, AAA partners with INRIX, a transportation data and insights company, to find out the best and worst times to travel over Labor Day weekend. INRIX analyzes real-world road data using a combination of preselected high-impact travel routes, multisource traffic info and a sophisticated statistical formula to create travel-delay predictions. The traffic info comes from GPS data, mobile apps, navigation services, roadside sensors and commercial fleet information.
It’s time to embrace the morning drive, travelers. This year’s Labor Day traffic will be lightest before either 10 a.m. or 1 p.m., depending on the day, from Thursday through Monday—though unlike last year, Sunday will be smooth sailing all day long.
Here are the best times to drive to and from your Labor Day destination. These times (and all times coming up) reflect your local time zone and the local time zone of the route described.
Again, mornings are your friend here. When it’s time to head back to civilization, fill up your trusty Buc-ee’s travel coffee mug and get out there before the mid to late afternoon. Luckily, Sunday is again a great travel day. Here are the worst times to hit the road this Labor Day weekend.
We have some new entries in this year’s list of the worst driving routes. AAA says three of the biggest destinations this year will be Seattle, Denver and Boston, so it’s no surprise that traffic there will be more congested than usual. To determine the worst routes, AAA and INRIX looked at just how much longer it will take to drive to popular Labor Day destinations compared to a typical day.
The biggest mover was Seattle, where Labor Day travelers will spend more than twice as long on the road to and from the Cascade Mountains. Bostonians heading to Providence, Rhode Island, for a beach weekend will also see their traffic times double.

articles.title: Here’s Why Tennis Balls Come in Sealed Cans … but Footballs and Baseballs Don’t
articles.content:
The U.S. Open is underway in New York, and once again I’m reminded that I should have practiced harder when I was a junior. But bygones! Let’s talk tennis balls. Specifically, the ones that come sealed in pop-top cans.
If you didn’t know, not all of them do. “There are two types of tennis ball: pressureless and pressurized,” says Rod Cross, a retired physics professor and an expert on the technology of tennis. (The name of one of his books is The Physics and Technology of Tennis.) It’s the pressurized ones that come in cans, and coming up, he’ll explain why.
But wait … footballs are pressurized, which just means that the air pressure inside the ball is higher than outside. So are basketballs. And volleyballs. And tons of other sports balls. But hardly any of them are sold in cans. To further the tennis-ball conundrum: “In the old days, when I was young, even pressurized balls were sold in cardboard boxes, [not cans],” Cross says.
It’s all too much for this weekend warrior. What happened in the tennis-ball-packaging world since the professor was a kid? The balls haven’t changed all that much. Ahead, Cross explains why tennis balls come in cans and lets us in on a few secrets of the science of tennis balls. Read on to learn more.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more fun facts, entertainment, cleaning, humor, travel and tech all week long.
It’s been nearly 100 years. When lawn tennis was established in the United States, starting around 1880, tennis balls were mostly sold in paper bags or cardboard boxes. In the late 1920s, the Pennsylvania Rubber Company, which later evolved into one of the biggest names in tennis, Penn, began selling tennis balls in sealed metal cans.
They came with a key that rolled back the top like a sardine can, and they could not be resealed. According to the International Tennis Hall of Fame, World War II’s metal shortages brought back cardboard for a while, and Cross remembers seeing them packed in boxes into the 1950s (the aforementioned “old days”).
Resealable lids came along in the 1950s and ’60s, and in 1972, pop-tops replaced the key. In the 1980s, companies switched to plastic cans.
Sealed cans allow manufacturers to control the pressure precisely inside the can, keeping tennis balls at their peak performance level for as long as possible. Here’s why using a can works best.
Pressurized tennis balls bounce because the air inside the ball is at a higher pressure than the outside atmosphere. As the ball hits your racket or the court, the pressurized air inside pushes against the rubber and helps it resist deformation (aka getting squashed), and the ball bounces.
“Normal atmospheric pressure is 14.7 psi, but the pressure inside the ball is about 27 to 29 psi,” Cross says. So sealing the can and injecting air under pressure keeps the balls in the exact environment they need to properly bounce. You can test this: Regulation hard-court tennis balls (called Type 2 or medium) must bounce back to between 53 and 58 inches when dropped from a height of 100 inches.
“Pressurized balls are sold in a pressured can to prevent the air from gradually leaking out through the porous rubber wall,” Cross says. Tennis balls have a hollow rubber core that is not airtight, and once that rubber core is formed and covered with fuzz, that’s it—there’s no way to pump them up like you can a football or soccer ball.
This is why pressureless balls, which bounce due to their thicker, stiffer rubber instead of an air-pressure differential, are popular for practice and in ball machines. “Pressureless balls last longer, since the air doesn’t leak out,” Cross says.
Sealed cans keep tennis balls fresher longer. Since a pressurized tennis ball loses air gradually, the old way of packing them in cardboard meant that by the time the balls arrived at the pro shop or sporting-goods store, they were already losing air and bounce. Players had to do a squeeze test to find good ones rather than have confidence that fresh balls were, well, fresh.
Today, that’s not a worry. Example: I have a few unopened cans of tennis balls in my garage. I bought a case months ago, and these are the stragglers. But I’m not worried in the least that they’ll be bad when I get to them. We’ll get to the specifics in the next section, but no matter how long it is, they’ll be infinitely more playable than if they had been sitting loose or in a cardboard box.
The Penn balls in my garage don’t have expiration dates, and I can’t find any indication that Wilsons do either. (Wilson is another big name in tennis.) So I suppose they could last indefinitely. But most tennis pros put the window of freshness on an unopened can at anywhere from six months to a year, with two years being the outside limit.
But after you crack it open, the countdown begins. “Once opened, balls in pressurized cans can still be used a few weeks later,” Cross says. But you won’t catch a pro using a three-week-old ball at Wimbledon. Those are more for you and me hitting around on a Sunday morning. Even then, after a few hard-play sessions, you’re going to notice a difference in the feel of the ball.
“At amateur-competition level, new balls are used for each morning or afternoon event, while at professional level, new balls are used after every nine games,” Cross says. As the ball gets smacked around, the felt cover gets fluffy and slows down the ball as it flies through the air. “That’s why professionals take three balls to serve, then throw away the most fluffy ball,” he adds.
That distinctive whoosh (which is always accompanied by that fresh tennis-ball smell) is the sound of the pressure being released from inside the can. As soon as you pop the top, the higher-pressure air inside the can rushes through the opening to the lower-pressure outside, creating sound waves that dissipate as the opening gets larger.
Yes. It won’t make it as good as new, but depending on your standards, it might be close enough. “Old balls can be repressurized by placing them in a pressurized container for a few days, but the outer felt cover will still be fluffy or worn down,” Cross says.
You can find basic pressurizers for less than $20 at Target and Tennis Warehouse, and more sophisticated versions online for about $75 and up.
No. “Pressureless balls are sold in a cardboard box,” Cross says. Since the air inside them is at regular atmospheric pressure, there’s no need to keep them in a pressurized can. You can also buy pressureless tennis balls in mesh bags, especially if you purchase in bulk.
Pressureless tennis balls were patented by Swedish shoe giant Tretorn in 1955, and Cross says they’re popular in Europe and South America. But we’re seeing more of them over here too. Due to environmental concerns over the use of plastic in pressurized tennis ball cans, Wilson developed a new pressureless ball called Triniti that mimics the livelier bounce, faster play and lighter “feel” of pressurized balls. These are sold in recyclable cardboard boxes.
Some do, but not many, and the reason is simple: “Other balls can be pumped up to the correct pressure with an air pump,” Cross says, though some balls don’t use air or pressure at all. Here’s how it breaks down.

Do all tennis balls come in cans?

No. “Pressureless balls are sold in a cardboard box,” Cross says. Since the air inside them is at regular atmospheric pressure, there’s no need to keep them in a pressurized can. You can also buy pressureless tennis balls in mesh bags, especially if you purchase in bulk.

Pressureless tennis balls were patented by Swedish shoe giant Tretorn in 1955, and Cross says they’re popular in Europe and South America. But we’re seeing more of them over here too. Due to environmental concerns over the use of plastic in pressurized tennis ball cans, Wilson developed a new pressureless ball called Triniti that mimics the livelier bounce, faster play and lighter “feel” of pressurized balls. These are sold in recyclable cardboard boxes.

Do other balls come in cans?

Some do, but not many, and the reason is simple: “Other balls can be pumped up to the correct pressure with an air pump,” Cross says, though some balls don’t use air or pressure at all. Here’s how it breaks down.

  • Padel balls: A very close cousin to the tennis ball, padel balls also have a hollow rubber core and a felt cover. They are sold under pressure in pop-top cans, but they are softer and have more give.
  • Racquetballs: The hollow, air-filled racquetball gets its bounce from the rubber shell, not the air inside (much like a pressureless tennis ball). So while they are often sold in cans to keep the rubber fresh, the cans are not pressurized.
  • Pickleballs: The nemesis of tennis players everywhere (I kid, pickleballers!), the plastic, Whiffle ball–like pickleball is hollow and has multiple holes, so it’s just sold in bags, boxes or other non-pressurized containers.
  • Footballs, soccer balls and basketballs: Larger air-filled balls are sold naked or in boxes and are filled using a bicycle pump or air compressor. (If you’ve ever searched your garage and junk drawers for hours looking for the pump’s needle attachment, you feel my pain.) These balls will eventually deflate, but give them a quick pump and you’ll be good to go.
  • Baseballs and golf balls: Solid-core balls do not have air inside at all, so there’s no need to sell or store them under pressure. They may get old and brittle, or lose performance capability after years of storage or use, but these balls won’t deflate.
